newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Swedes, once free riders, undecided on EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Swedes, once free riders, undecided on EMU.

text.p: A dramatic economic turnaround has put it on track to meet entry conditions, but Sweden is still months if not years away from deciding whether it wants to join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
With the ruling Social Democrats lacking direction and split on the issue, sentiment in a country with a long tradition of independence and neutrality is fairly evenly balanced for and against EMU.
"We are a nation of free riders outside the walls, trading with both sides," said Jan Herin, chief economist for the Swedish Employers' Confederation.
"Things are gradually changing and we are becoming more European, but the feeling of staying outside and seeing how we get on goes deep," he told Reuters.
Prime Minister Goran Persson and his Finance Minister Erik Asbrink have quietly tiptoed away from their positive stance on EMU one year ago and are now uncommitted.

"If they are in favour, they should say so, if not, they should also say so. For many people, their final view will be dictated by the opinion of leading politicians," said Kjell-Olof Feldt, a much-respected and pro-Europe former finance minister.
Herin and Handelsbanken chief economist Carl Hamilton were agreed that the Social Democratic leadership would probably formulate its position in May/June 1997 ahead of a party congress in September.
Swedes appeared unimpressed by the fact that the Italian lira re-entered the Exchange Rate Mechanism in November, leaving Sweden one of only three countries outside the ERM.
These are "Britain, which doesn't want to join, Greece which can't, and Sweden which thinks it doesn't need to," the tabloid Expressen commented.
In fact Swedish opposition to EMU grew to 44 percent of 1,000 people questioned in November and December, from 38 percent opposed in October, according to the polling organisation Temo.
Less than one third of Swedes were positive about EMU and the rest were undecided.
While the SDP remained uncommitted, the opposition Conservatives and Liberals were nominally in favour of EMU and the Greens, Centre, Christian Democrats and Leftists against.

Even if the Social Democratic leaders finally decide to lead the party and country into EMU from the front, political commentators said they cannot count on a majority in the 349-seat Riksdag, the single-chamber Swedish parliament.
A government-appointed panel headed by university professor Lars Calmfors said in early November that the arguments against EMU entry in 1999 were stronger than those in favour.

"It would not take much to tip the balance," he told a seminar in Stockholm on November 29. "If it were only Sweden and Greece that did not join, it would be hard for Sweden to stay out in the long run."
ANGUISHED DEBATE ABOUT JOINING EU

Neutral through two world wars and non-aligned in peacetime, Sweden was a unique beneficiary of the terms of trade when Europe needed rebuilding and prospered on the northern fringe of the continent after 1945.

Its labour market came to be known as the Swedish model and was the envy of the world. The twin towers of the LO trade union headquarters in Stockholm were a reassuring symbol of harmony between organised labour and the ruling SDP.

By the late 1980s, however, Sweden's high wages and ever more generous benefits had begun to seriously undermine its competitiveness. Deregulation of capital markets led to a financial boom and bust, the collapse of communism redefined the need for neutrality and suddenly Europe beckoned.
Swedish voters' scepticism may stem from the back-door way in which the government in 1990 announced it would seek membership of the European Economic Community (EEC).

The momentous decision to abandon centuries of independence was buried halfway down a list of action points to tackle an economic crisis which one newspaper called the "most infamous footnote in Swedish history."

Swedish industry leaders from blue-chip companies like Ericsson, Volvo and Electrolux feel that although Sweden is in the European Economic Area -- grouping the EU and some of the old European Free Trade Area (EFTA) -- it needs to be more of an insider if its voice is to be heard.
Economists say Sweden has raised such a monster of state interference in the economy that it would need the external discipline of Brussels to bring its finances in order.

In the debate about Europe, loss of neutrality, environmental concerns, fears about lower welfare benefits and the harmful effects of a more liberal policy on alcohol were set against fears of Swedish export industries losing access to European markets.
SWEDEN COULD MEET EMU CRITERIA
In a referendum in 1994 Swedes voted narrowly in favour of joining the EU from January 1, 1995. Now, three out of five of the economic convergence criteria for EMU are as good as achieved.
Sweden currently has the best inflation record of any EU country. Consumer prices actually fell 0.3 percent in November to give a year-on-year disinflation of 0.3 percent.

Handelsbanken -- one of the country's three biggest commercial banks -- has predicted a budget deficit in 1997 of 1.6 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) after 2.5 percent in 1995, and state debt falling as a percentage of GDP to 74 percent from 77 percent.
This would put Sweden well within the three percent deficit/GDP ratio required by the Maastricht treaty, but leave it outside the 60 percent debt to GDP ratio.

On the interest rate front, the Riksbank's repurchase rate which leads other interest rates in the economy has fallen steadily in the last 12 months to 4.10 percent now and some money market analysts forecast it could dip below four percent.

Sweden needed to place its crown inside the ERM by the end of 1996 to pass the fifth test, a stable two-year stint inside the currency grid, but politicians and Riksbank officials said in November it was "not an issue on the table at present."

Sweden argues that its currency can be stable outside the ERM, while Germany's Bundesbank insists that currencies which are to become part of the single currency, the euro, should enter the grid for two years.
Unlike Britain and Denmark, Sweden has no opt-out clause on EMU and its position on currency stability has raised eyebrows.

But visiting Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on November 27 in Stockholm he could not see a problem of Sweden's qualifying for EMU if it had met the convergence criteria even if was outside the ERM.

Inside or outside EMU, Sweden will have to amend its constitution in line with Maastricht requirements, changing the contract of the Riksbank governor, establishing the central bank's already effective independence and removing its authority to issue banknotes.

Economics professor Johan Lybeck said in October the government was playing a difficult political game, but skilfully, and he concluded, "I'm certain Sweden will join by 2002 when it's time to pool currencies."
